title: Tragedy of the commons

definition.text: The idea that when people share a resource that benefits each user at a cost to everyone, each person has a reason to overuse it, so together they use it up.

facts.text: English economist William Forster Lloyd described the problem in an 1833 pamphlet about herders sharing a common pasture, where adding extra cattle could lead to overgrazing.
The name comes from a 1968 essay in the journal Science by ecologist Garrett Hardin, who took his title from Lloyd's pamphlet.
Hardin's main worry was human overpopulation, and he wrote that 'freedom in a commons brings ruin to all'.
The commons problem is used as a model for many resource problems today, including water, forests, fish, and oil, gas and coal.
Climate change has been described as a huge example of the tragedy, with the Earth treated as a commons whose resources are depleted without regard to the harm done to others.
Proposed government fixes include privatization, regulation such as permits for fishing or logging, and making users pay for the harm they cause.

Elinor Ostrom and colleagues found the tragedy less common and easier to solve than Hardin claimed, because local users often design their own rules; a Swiss Alpine commons has been run by farmers since 1517.
Critics note that historical English common land always had a legal owner, and only people with legal rights, called commoners, could use it.

related: Ostrom's design principles for the commons
contested_note: Scholars dispute whether overuse is inevitable: Ostrom's work is seen by some economists as refuting Hardin, and others say open, unregulated common land never really existed.

title: Commons dilemma

definition.text: A kind of social dilemma in which people's short-term selfish interests clash with the long-term interests of the group and the common good.

facts.text: Researchers study, in the laboratory and the field, when groups under- or over-harvest common resources.
When people harvest in a fixed order, those who go first take more than those who follow.
People take less from a common pool when others can see them than when they act anonymously.
Selective punishments for overuse, such as installing water and electricity meters in houses, can encourage conservation.

distinct_from: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons

title: Comedy of the commons
article: Tragedy of the commons#Comedy of the commons

definition.text: The case where a shared resource becomes more valuable to each user the more people use it, so 'the more the merrier'.

facts.text: Legal scholar Carol M. Rose described the idea in a 1986 article, giving commerce and group recreation as examples.
Rose argued that such 'comedic' public resources are more likely to suffer from too little investment than from overuse.

distinct_from: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons

title: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons

definition.text: The range of ways, from local self-organized rules to government action, proposed for stopping people from overusing a shared resource.

facts.text: Finding solutions to the tragedy of the commons is counted among the main problems of political philosophy.
Turning a common resource into private property gives the new owner a reason to keep it productive, an idea linked to Coase in 1960.
Privatization works when the owner pays the full price of using up the resource.
Governments can cap how much of a shared resource any one person may use, for example through permits for mining, fishing, hunting, grazing and logging.
Government solutions are used when a community is too large for its social ties to hold it together.
A middle way shares ownership between government and community, so that no one or two parties hold all the power.
Political scientist Robert Axelrod argues that even self-interested people often find ways to cooperate, because restraint serves both them and the group.

related: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

title: Common-pool resource

definition.text: A natural or human-made resource system, such as fishing grounds or an irrigation system, that is costly but not impossible to keep people from using.

facts.text: Unlike pure public goods, common-pool resources get crowded or overused because what one user takes is no longer there for others.
Examples include forests, irrigation systems, fishing grounds, groundwater basins, pastures and the atmosphere.
Without management, each fisher has a reason to catch as many fish as possible before someone else does, so fish stocks soon run down.
They may be owned by governments as public goods, by communities as common property, or by individuals and firms as private goods; when no one owns them they are open access.
Elinor Ostrom found many such resources run by local self-managing communities, contradicting the claim that they must be privatized or be destroyed.
In James Bay, Quebec, beaver numbers recovered after Indigenous communities' customary hunting laws were legally recognized and outside trappers were banned.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

title: Resource stock and flow

definition.text: The split of a shared resource into a core stock that must be protected and a flow of units, such as fish or grass, that can be harvested from it.

facts.text: As long as the stock is not harmed, it keeps regrowing the flow, so careful use can continue indefinitely.
Taking more than the flow shrinks the stock, which in turn shrinks future flows; sometimes the loss cannot be undone.
A pasture can be grazed a certain amount each year without harm, but overgrazing makes it prone to erosion and less useful.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

title: Common property regime

definition.text: A social arrangement by which a community regulates how a shared resource is kept up, maintained and used.

facts.text: It is not the same thing as a common-pool resource, since such resources are not always governed as common property.
Such systems arise when users acting alone threaten the total benefit of the resource, and they protect the core resource while sharing out what can be harvested.
Community members have monitored access, while outsiders can be kept out, so the resource looks private to outsiders and common to insiders.
Rules must limit the amount, timing and technology of harvesting: limits set too high destroy the resource, and limits set too low waste benefits.

related: Ostrom's design principles for the commons
distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

title: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

definition.text: Eight conditions that Elinor Ostrom found in long-lasting community arrangements for managing shared resources.

facts.text: The first principles are clearly defined boundaries, and rules for taking and supplying the resource that fit local conditions.
Most users should take part in making the rules, and monitors should be users themselves or answer to them.
Rule-breakers face sanctions that grow step by step, and conflicts can be settled cheaply and easily.
Authorities such as the government must at least recognize the users' right to organize, and large resources are run as layers of nested groups with small local ones at the base.
Ostrom set out this work in Governing the Commons (1990), showing that communities around the world have managed shared resources successfully through local governance.

title: Adaptive governance of common-pool resources

definition.text: A way of managing shared resources that Ostrom recommended for problems that are complex, uncertain and fragmented.

facts.text: Because management depends on the type of resource, a strategy that works in one place may not suit another.
Ostrom's five requirements are good timely information, ways to handle conflict, users who help monitor rule-keeping, flexible infrastructure, and readiness to adapt and fix errors.

prerequisites: Ostrom's design principles for the commons
distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

title: Open access resource

definition.text: A resource that no one owns and that anyone can use, where what one person takes leaves less for others.

facts.text: Open access goods need little oversight or are hard to restrict, and because they are first come, first served, they are prone to the tragedy of the commons.
In an open fishery, profits draw in more fishers, leaving fewer fish; scarcer fish raise prices, which draws in still more fishers.
Hardin's work has been criticized for failing to tell common-pool resources apart from open access resources.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

title: Four types of goods

definition.text: A grid that sorts goods by two questions, whether people can be kept from using them and whether one person's use leaves less for others.

facts.text: Goods that can be withheld and are used up, such as food, clothing and parking spaces, are private goods.
Goods that cannot be withheld but are used up, such as fish stocks and timber, are common-pool resources.
Goods that can be withheld but are not used up, such as cinemas, software and private parks, are club goods.
Goods that cannot be withheld and are not used up, such as free-to-air television, air and national defense, are public goods.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons
